stories.title_en: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen

comments.author: vessenes
comments.text:
This is insane.
Astra can, without tooling, determine what games small networks are trained on, can edit the weights of networks directly to improve outcomes, and can hand edit a small qwen model to improve its math skills by like 5x.
I'm shook. If you'd asked me this morning whether LLMs have native understanding of their weights that is less than human <-> neuron understanding, the same as human or more than human, I would have said "same to less" depending on definitions.
No human can go edit a brain to become better at math. This is just very, very surprising to me and extremely interesting. I would guess this upsets quite a number of interp theories and philosophical takes on what's going on with these networks.

comments.author: xg15
comments.text:
And here we go...
As others have said, while still absolutely insane, I don't find it completely out-of-the-blue surprising. One of the recurring abilities of (current-generation) LLMs seem to be to rapidly grasp very complex systems, where humans would need months or years to reach the same level of expertise.
You can see this in the way a coding agent can "understand" and explain sprawling legacy codebases in seconds.
You can also see it in the projects that are using them to reverse-engineer proprietary IoT protocols or computer games.
But those were all systems where we had detailed knowledge about what structures are there to be reverse-enginered.
If the models can transfer this ability to some other systems where we
don't
know the underlying structure then I think we will be in for a lot more craziness in the future. (Protein interaction networks? DNA sequences? Ecosystem interactions? Animal languages?)
As for weights, if the models really can analyze the semantics behind specific weights or directions, I have my hopes that they could also give a textual explanation or help designing tools to make "handcrafting" weights more practical in general.

comments.text:
I think the subfield has been there for a long time. See a small section of papers on the topic of generating dynamic weights during inference, predicting weights from network architecture, and learning the distribution of previously trained network parameters, just to name a few keywords:
Parameter Prediction for Unseen Deep Architectures [1]
NeuroGen: Neural Network Parameter Generation via Large Language Models [2]
Diffusion-Based Neural Network Weights Generation [3]
The critical thing to me is that Astra is capable of doing it. I don't know if it was trained to do so.
All this does not make it any less crazy in my books. And I still don't know how I can sleep easy tonight.

comments.author: NitpickLawyer
comments.text:
> As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop [13]. When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights
HA! Now that's cool. Not necessarily the improvements, those are ancient and probably overtrained benchmarks, but it's so cool that the model found a singular direction for this "loop bug". I imagine it could possibly do much the same thing in finding other "single directions" on a variety of topics (if allowed by guardrails). This is really really cool, especially for the mechinterp folks.

comments.author: vanyle
comments.text:
I don't think this is an emergent capability. I think Astra was trained on neural weights data as an attempt by OpenAI to get to recursive self improvement.
Something similar happen in early GPT models which had a lot of chess game in standard notation in their training data which made them very good at chess as long as your prompt had the right format.
We'll see if this attempt at RSI worked.

comments.author: fancyfredbot
comments.text:
For the tiny models with a few thousand weights, it seems plausible Astra can actually understand what the network detects and figure out it's e.g. a triangle detector. This is possibly helped by the existence of many breakout playing networks on the web.
For Qwen, even the smallest versions like 3.5-0.8B it's becoming less plausible that it could be interpreted in a forward pass, even with reasoning. I'm wondering if the result here is recalled from many examples of instruction tuned versions of this model.
A smaller Gemma model doesn't fare as well but unclear whether this is due to fewer users and less weight examples or because it's already very well trained.

comments.author: jsenn
comments.text:
I feel like this is conflating 2 separate results in a slightly misleading way.
> We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights
This claim is backed up by the ability of Astra, given a text representation of the weights of tiny (20k) special-purpose models, to figure out what those models do and in some cases improve them beyond what RL could do
just by reading the weights with no tool calls
. They call this "weight-space programming".
> Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights
Here it did use tool calls, and seemingly used standard steering vector techniques to identify and fix reasoning loops in this small Qwen model. This doesn't seem that related to the previous results.

comments.author: gregates
comments.text:
This article misleads by presenting these transitions as from "popular boys name" to "popular girls name", when in fact most of the cases here are from "rare name, sometimes used for boys and sometimes girls" to "suddenly trendy for girls".
To take Ashley as an example. This name suddenly started ramping up in popularity in the 60s. In 1970, there were 927 girls named Ashley in the U.S. It peaked at 54,856 in 1987.
It became notably more popular for boys at roughly the same time! The peak of M Ashley was in 1980, at 746. (Note: it's also very likely that these numbers are wrong. The SSA data also has 56 male Marys in 1980, which is likely the result of coding error.)
Meanwhile, in 1945, solidly in the time period when the article would like you believe that Ashley was solidly a boys name, there were 57 M Ashleys and 10 F. 1950 was 55 M/15 F. Prior to 1960, a "good" year for Ashley was around 100 total babies, with some split of both M and F.
To me, a more honest interpretation of this data is that Ashley was a somewhat unisex, but mostly just very uncommon, name that suddenly became trendy in the 1960s, especially for girls but also for boys.
